endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Data management must be grounded in an effective data mapping exercise and a strong, clear, and efficient data governance process.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Breach Notification: Timely reporting (typically within 10–15 days) of any impermissible use, disclosure, or security incident.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Inventory all third-party entities with access to organizational content and establish approved GAI technology and service provider lists.

endorsements.title: AI-augmented frameworks for enhancing Alzheimer's disease clinical trials: A memory clinic perspective
endorsements.issuer: The journal of prevention of Alzheimer's disease
endorsements.quote: This includes auditing data flows for HIPAA/GDPR compliance, encrypting digital biomarkers, and collaborating on de-identified datasets, practices that can reduce breach risks and foster trust via transparent, opt-in data policies.

endorsements.title: ONRAMP-AI-VRAR: an operational protocol for ethics and governance of AI-enabled immersive psychotherapy
endorsements.quote: Using ONRAMP-AI-VRAR’s Data Flow Mapping Template, systems must ensure encryption, anonymization, access controls and comply with HIPAA, GDPR, and CCPA if U.S.-based, or EU MDR/AI Act if international.

endorsements.title: Ethical considerations for multimodal artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Tracking the trajectories of latent embeddings, derived risk scores, synthetic images, or other model-generated attributes creates shared accountability by documenting where they originate, how they are transformed, and where they are ultimately used.

evidence.title: Clinician-led, AI-assisted clinical software development: multi-domain verification of a deployed ePROM application
evidence.outcome: Undocumented third-party data flow found by code audit versus privacy claim
evidence.effect: A third-party analytics tag contradicted the app's local-only privacy claim.
evidence.quote: Technical findings included instrument mislabelling, a manifest that failed installability validation, and a third-party analytics tag contradicting the local-only privacy claim.
evidence.sample_unit: single application case; 78 scoring test cases, 52 usability participants (14 clinicians, 26 patients, 12 older adults), 926 author messages, 23 storage canaries

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether mapping AI data flows, third parties, and legal agreements reduces data exposure. One deployment audit found an undocumented third-party analytics tag that contradicted an app's local-only privacy claim, so the hazard is documented but the practice has not been evaluated.

perspectives.view: Six sources endorse the practice, all frameworks or commentaries, and no comparative or observational study measures its effect on exposure or breach rates. The single supplied study is a hazard report of level 3 evidence with sample size not reported. Under GRADE conventions, certainty for the practice itself cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

A code audit in a real deployment found a third-party analytics tag sending data despite a local-only privacy claim. This suggests vendor statements alone may miss exposures. Whether a data flow map made before deployment would have caught this tag is untested, since the finding came from a code audit rather than from documentation review.

The audited tag surfaced only through inspection of code, which suggests that maps built from vendor questionnaires or contracts may not reflect runtime behavior. No study reports how long mapping takes, how often maps drift from actual traffic, or whether plugins added after go-live are captured.

CHAI playbooks tie data governance to breach notification within 10 to 15 days, and NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to inventory third parties with access to content. A current map may help an organization determine what was disclosed and to whom when a notification deadline applies, though no study has measured this.

The audited app told users their data stayed on the device while a third-party tag operated in the background. Patients generally cannot inspect code, so they depend on the organization to confirm privacy claims. An unverified claim of this kind may reduce trust once it is discovered.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare organizations or AI deployments with and without structured data flow mapping, measuring undocumented third-party transmissions found at audit, breach incidents, time to breach notification, and staff effort. Such studies should also test whether maps built from documentation match network or code-level observation over time.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The one hazard study involved older adults and did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants, so there is no evidence on whether mapping protects these groups or whether their apps and vendors differ in third-party exposure.
